F=ma Problem Series
Lesson 5: Collisions
jonjoseph 2025-07-09 19:32:17 t V
This week we'll take the lessons we learned about momentum and energy and apply them to collisions - a commonly-tested topic on the F=ma.
jonjoseph 2025-07-09 19:32:27 t V
Our big idea this week is to ask yourself a few key questions as you think about a problem. These are questions that work for almost any F=ma problem, and can help focus your thinking.
jonjoseph 2025-07-09 19:32:40 t V
Some examples:

-Which physical principles apply?

-What information do I have?

-What information am I trying to find?

-Is it clear that the provided information is sufficient?

jonjoseph 2025-07-09 20:54:03 t V
The problem implies that mechanical energy is conserved when it states that the block slides "smoothly" onto the slope. It also tells us that the motion is frictionless.
jonjoseph 2025-07-09 20:54:14 t V

jonjoseph 2025-07-09 20:54:46 t V
So the problem gives us the initial masses and velocities of two objects moving in one dimension, and we apply momentum conservation and energy conservation to figure out what happens after they interact. Is there any substantial difference from a perfectly elastic collision problem?

There really isn't. If we were interested in something like how high the small block rises on the sloped block, the fact that this isn't truly a collision would matter. But here, we're just interested in the final velocities.

All the initial information and all the physical principles involved are the same as for an elastic collision, so the answer to the problem will be exactly the same as for an elastic collision.

jonjoseph 2025-07-09 21:03:52 t V
Summary
jonjoseph 2025-07-09 21:03:55 t V
When solving a problem, it's often helpful to begin reviewing:

- What information the problem provides

- What information you want to find

- Whether the provided information is obviously sufficient to solve the problem, even if you don't know the details of how it will be done
jonjoseph 2025-07-09 21:03:58 t V
Collisions problems come in several types. They may be perfectly elastic, in which case kinetic/potential energy is conserved during the collision. If they are completely inelastic, the objects that collide stick together, and we can usually solve them using momentum conservation alone. Collisions can also be intermediate between these two extremes (as you'll see on the homework).
jonjoseph 2025-07-09 21:04:03 t V
Collisions can also occur entirely in one dimension, or in two dimensions (or three, if there are more than two objects involved).
jonjoseph 2025-07-09 21:04:07 t V
All collisions obey conservation of momentum.
jonjoseph 2025-07-09 21:04:11 t V
Changing reference frames commonly simplifies collision problems. In many problems, the center of mass frame is especially easy to analyze.
jonjoseph 2025-07-09 21:04:18 t V
In perfectly-elastic collisions in one dimension, the difference in velocities between the objects stays the same magnitude and switches sign from before to after the collision.
